title: Optimal acceleration from predetermined gradient-descent stepsizes
statement: For x_t=x_(t-1)-eta_t grad f(x_(t-1)), with positive deterministic stepsizes chosen before the run, determine the sharp asymptotic worst-case last-iterate objective-gap rate on all finite-dimensional convex L-smooth functions admitting a minimizer. Write R_N for the gap normalized by L||x_0-x_*||^2, taking its supremum over dimension, objective, minimizer x_* and initial point x_0 outside the minimizer set. In the known-horizon setting, minimize this supremum over length-N schedules; in the anytime setting, require one infinite schedule to satisfy its guarantee at every stopping time.
source_locator: Jung, Cho and Yun, equation (1), Theorems 1.1-1.2 and Section 5; Altschuler and Parrilo, Sections 1-3; Zhang et al., publisher abstract.
status_basis: The September 2026 paper leaves the sharp rates unresolved. The scoped later-work search found no matching resolution or correction. Acceleration beyond 1/N is already known in both settings.
plain_summary: How much speed can gradient descent gain by changing only its predetermined step lengths? The answer would identify a basic limit of this widely used optimization method.
assumptions: Exact gradients, Euclidean norm and unconstrained smooth convex minimization; no strong-convexity assumption.
No momentum, averaging, randomization or adaptation to observations. Stepsizes may exceed 2/L. The normalization uses a minimizer x_* and a starting point x_0 outside the minimizer set.
The guarantee concerns the final iterate, not the best iterate. Constants must be uniform over the stated function class and dimension.
scope: Two related rates are recorded together to prevent conflation. A known-horizon schedule may depend on N; an anytime schedule cannot depend on its future stopping time. Quadratic-only or stochastic-gradient results answer different questions.
target: Close or narrow one of the two source-reported rate gaps, specifying which setting is addressed.
success_criteria: An upper bound needs a schedule and a uniform proof; a lower bound must quantify over every permitted schedule.
State exponents exactly and preserve logarithmic factors, constants, horizon restrictions and limit quantifiers.
Finite computations or fitted slopes alone do not establish an asymptotic rate.
known_results: Let a=log_2(1+sqrt(2)) and b=log_2(1+sqrt(3)). The silver construction gives O(N^-a) at terminal lengths N=2^k-1; the September 2026 paper records this best-known non-anytime exponent and reports Omega(N^-b) for every length-N schedule.
For anytime schedules, the published upper exponent is 2a/(1+a). The later barrier is limsup_N N^(2b/(1+b)) R_N >= c for a universal c>0.
These are different optimization problems; the anytime barrier is not a lower bound at every N.
prerequisites: Smooth convex optimization and worst-case oracle complexity.
Uniform asymptotic estimates and proof certificates for optimization inequalities.
significance: Determines how much acceleration can come from stepsizes alone. Relevance to optimization theory is direct; benefits for nonconvex training require separate evidence.
